title: Al-Shifa bint Abdullah
hookLine: who taught writing and, reports say, oversaw the market

cards: Who taught the Prophet's wife to write? The answer turns up in an unlikely place, a chapter of hadith about medicine and charms. A room in Medina.
Hafsah, one of the wives of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is sitting with a woman named al-Shifa.

The Prophet walks in, sees them together, and says something that only makes sense if everyone in the room already knows a small fact. Today: al-Shifa, daughter of Abdullah, and the fact the Prophet took for granted.

teach.h: TEACH HER THE CHARM FOR SORES.
teach.b: The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, told by al-Shifa herself.
She was with Hafsah when the Prophet came in, and he said: won't you teach her the charm for skin sores, as you taught her writing? One sentence, and look at what it holds.

Al-Shifa knew a healing recitation, the kind people said over a painful rash, and the Prophet asked her to pass it on. In the same breath, almost in passing, he mentions that she had already taught Hafsah to write.

He doesn't praise it as unusual. He uses it as the model: do this the way you did that. A woman teaching a woman to write, in the Prophet's own household, and his response is: good, now teach her this too.
Her name, al-Shifa, is the Arabic word for healing, which fits the charm. But the line that lasts is the other one. She taught writing.
Later reports, in biographical works compiled long after, say the caliph Umar gave her a role in the market of Medina, keeping an eye on trade.
Some scholars accept those reports, some doubt them, and the details differ, so hold that part lightly.
The firm part is the room with Hafsah, and a teacher whose teaching the Prophet simply assumed.
No speech about learning, no ceremony. Just one person who could write, sitting with one person who couldn't yet, until she could.

how: Muslims remember al-Shifa from a report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, where the Prophet asks her to teach Hafsah a healing charm as she had taught her writing; later biographical works add that she had a role in the market.

games.q: you are the Prophet. you walk in and find a woman who knows a healing charm sitting with your wife. what do you say?
o: ask her to teach your wife the charm, as she taught her writing.
games.why: Abu Dawud keeps his words: won't you teach her the charm, as you taught her writing? the writing lesson was already a given.

practice: Remember who first taught you letters, a parent's finger under a word, a teacher, an older sibling, and thank them in your heart.
Then think of someone who could use a reader beside them, a child sounding out a sign or a parent with a confusing form. If you pray, you can ask for patience to teach well.

wordCard.voice: Al-Shifa, healing, the woman the Prophet asked to teach a charm against skin sores, as she had already taught Hafsah, his wife, to write. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: she taught writing. The Prophet took it for granted. See you tomorrow.
